title: ITD 132 Quiz 1 Study Guide
description: Relational database concepts, keys, indexes and views, SELECT and JOIN, the system catalog, and MySQL data types, in the same order as the quiz and flashcards.

blocks.text: Everything lives in tables
A relational database management system (RDBMS) keeps all its data in **tables** made of **rows** and **columns**. Tables are related to each other through **keys**.

items: Each column has one **datatype** (integer, text, date...), and every value in it must fit that type.
Each row holds exactly **one value per column**: no lists in a cell.
The **order** of rows and columns has no meaning.
Each table is about **one subject** (patients, products, customers). A fact is entered once, which removes redundancy and inconsistency.

blocks.text: Formal and informal names

blocks.label: Remember:
blocks.text: Two departments that both need customer details share **one** customer table. Copying the data into each department's own table is exactly what the relational design avoids.
Primary key (PK)

items: Every table must have one. If none is declared, all the columns together become the key.

blocks.text: Composite primary key

When no single column identifies a row but a combination does, the key is made of **several columns**. An order-lines table with `order_id`, `product_id`, `quantity` and `ship_date` needs `order_id` + `product_id`.
Foreign key (FK)

A column whose values **refer to the primary key** of another table. It is what relates rows in two tables. Its name may differ from the key it points to, and its value must match an existing PK value.

rows: The table that **holds the foreign key**
The table whose **primary key is pointed to**

blocks.label: Watch out:
blocks.text: An order with `customer_id = 7` when no customer 7 exists is a broken relationship. The FK must refer to a PK value that is actually there.
Beyond tables

rows: Lets the database find rows by a column's value quickly, like a book's index
Speeds up lookups; **transparent** to the user
A **virtual table** computed from base tables when accessed
A routine saved in the database that can take **parameters**
A special stored procedure that **fires automatically** on insert, update or delete
Maintains business rules, e.g. an audit record

blocks.label: Remember:
blocks.text: The tables that actually hold the data are **base tables**. A view is computed from them each time it is used.

sections.name: 4. SQL Queries and the System Catalog

blocks.text: SELECT

SELECT title, price      -- which columns
FROM book                 -- which table
WHERE price > 15;         -- which rows
JOIN

A join links rows from two or more tables by comparing **key columns** (an FK to the PK it refers to) and returning the rows that match. It produces a result; it does **not** merge or change the tables.

SELECT gadget.gadget_title, maker.maker_name
FROM gadget JOIN maker ON gadget.maker_id = maker.maker_id;
Other SQL statements

rows: Builds or removes tables, views and other objects

blocks.text: The system catalog

Every database has **system tables** (the **data dictionary** or **system catalog**) holding **metadata**: data about data, such as the tables, columns and users. You read them but **never alter them directly**.
Why types exist

The same bits can be a number, text or a date. The type is the contract that says which, reserves the right space, rejects nonsense, and enables correct sorting, math and date arithmetic. **Rule of thumb: pick the smallest, most specific type that faithfully represents the data.**
Numeric

rows: -128 to 127 (0 to 255 unsigned); good for flags
about ±9.2 quintillion; for IDs that may exceed 2 billion
**Approximate**; avoid for currency (0.1 + 0.2 may not be 0.3)

blocks.text: `UNSIGNED` means no negative values, which doubles the positive range.
String

rows: Pads to a fixed length; best for uniform values such as codes
Up to 65,535 bytes; the default for most text
TINY to LONG, 255 bytes to 4 GB; indexes poorly
Like CHAR / VARCHAR but raw bytes
**One** value from a fixed list; hard to alter later
**Zero or more** values from a predefined list

blocks.text: `utf8mb4` uses up to **4 bytes per character**.
Date and time

rows: HH:MM:SS; can hold durations beyond 24 hours
Date and time, literal value, no time zone conversion, wide range
Stored as UTC, converted to the session time zone; **1970 to 2038**

blocks.label: Watch out:
blocks.text: Never store dates as strings: you lose sorting, validation and date arithmetic. `JSON` is a native type for flexible, semi-structured documents, but do not use it where a proper relational column would do.
